title: Cubs-Cardinals game delayed by Fourth of July fog at Wrigley Field
content:
CHICAGO — At 10:03 p.m. CT on the Fourth of July, a nationally televised game between the Chicago Cubs and St. Louis Cardinals was paused for what officials at Wrigley Field described as a fog delay.

The iconic ballpark, which opened in 1914, has long been known as an unpredictable venue, given its proximity to Lake Michigan and location in a dense residential neighborhood. From one inning to the next, the playing conditions can completely change. The weather elements and energy from the fans can be that volatile.

On Saturday night, the visibility faded to a point where the old-school scoreboard above the center-field bleachers could not be seen from the press box high atop the Friendly Confines. After six innings, the crowd of 38,872 watching two historic rivals sat through a 15-minute delay.

“At least from our perspective, the upper deck disappeared, the flag in center field disappeared,” Cubs manager Craig Counsell said after a 3-0 loss to the Cardinals. “The umpires did a good job. Honestly, it didn’t affect the game. It didn’t affect anything that happened in the game.”

The first pitch of the game from Cubs starter Shota Imanaga had already been pushed back 59 minutes due to lightning and heavy rain, and JJ Wetherholt lifted that 90.8 mph fastball into the basket above the left-field wall for a leadoff home run.

For the Cubs, the fog was the only memorable part of a forgettable game in which their offense produced zero runs against St. Louis starter Kyle Leahy (five innings) and four different relievers. When play resumed in the seventh inning, the loud crackle of fireworks could be heard in the distance.

“Wrigley will give you all the elements,” said Cubs left fielder Ian Happ, the club’s longest-tenured player. “We’ve had fog roll in before — I’ve never seen it that thick. It got to the point where it wasn’t playable.”

The most-talked-about play was the sliding catch that Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong made in the sixth inning before the fog delay. As Masyn Winn hit what would normally be a routine flyball, the Gold Glove defender backpedaled toward the warning track, readjusted and then dove forward onto his right knee to grab the out.

“That was brutal,” Crow-Armstrong said. “I’ve really never been a part of anything like that. It was reminiscent of when I was a kid playing rec-ball soccer.

“We were all kind of looking at each other like, ‘Let’s just talk and be loud and we’ll see what happens.’”

Winn, who once played with Crow-Armstrong as part of USA Baseball’s national youth program, told reporters: “I really don’t understand how PCA saw my ball, to be honest with you.”

It felt like an only-in-Wrigleyville moment.

“(The fog) rolled in and rolled out periodically,” Crow-Armstrong said. “A ball went up, and one of their guys thought it was hit to him and it was on the other side of the field. That tells you all you need to know.”
